Prove the fixed-M greedy for Subtransmutation: process sizes from M down to 1, require have[i] >= need[i], consume need[i], and transmute every excess unit at size i into sizes i-A and i-B whenever those sizes are positive. Explain why keeping excess at a larger size can never help later.

Review the Subtransmutation feasibility logic before coding. Confirm the monotonicity of candidate M, the correctness of descending processing, and the stopping or impossibility conditions when the contest's maximum candidate bound is exhausted.

Implement the Python solution for Subtransmutation by iterating candidate M values in increasing order, maintaining an array of available counts for the current simulation, and applying the descending greedy check until the first feasible M is found or all allowed candidates fail.
Test Subtransmutation on already-matching single-size targets, impossible targets, A = B cases, and tiny instances compared with a brute-force BFS over reachable multisets for very small bounds.
Produce the final, complete, self-contained Python solution incorporating all feedback. Return ONLY the code inside a single ```python fenced block. No explanation, no commentary.
